citations.review_text: Couldn't get the game to start. "Crimson Desert not responding" every time. Still couldn't figure out the issue. Tried just about every solution available online and I have an open ticket with Pearl Abyss.

this is the dumbest hundred dollar game I've ever wasted money on. 

won't let you launch without a controller, a PC GAME, and finally I was able to get it to launch without a controller, and it does this trippy cube modern art shit for about 20 minutes after hitting new game and then it crashes. 

and that's not even mentioning this fuckers 160 gig size. ridiculous. devs need to be flogged.

Heard good things about it lately, and love myself a long RPG to get lost in. However this game's storyline is apparently just about IRL crashing. It's about how the main character in the game attempts to do something in his world that will somehow break windows, steam and my sanity. This game managed to make it all of 15 minutes in my longest session before crashing yet again. I will not fondly remember my time with Crimson Crashing, or it's DLC Crimson BSOD. Would recommend finding something that manages to run stable-ish, and I say that as someone who played fallout 3 and New Vegas.

The NVIDIA GPU got it running at the very least, but kept crashing on either a cutscene, or going through the menu tabs. I had heard they fixed a lot of the problems early on, but I haven't gotten to barely touch the game because it was poorly optimized from the start and apparently whatever they did wasn't enough to work across the board still so this ended up being a waste of 70 bucks. Use my review as a possibility if you decide to buy this game.

claims.claim: Movement keys such as WASD are hardlocked and cannot be remapped in the settings.

citations.review_text:
I refunded the game. I cannot REMAP the movement keys from WASD to ARROW KEYS. As a left handed gamer, this is a must for me. It is unbelievable that in 2026, a game does not allow to rebind WASD keys to ARROW KEYS. And I do not want to waste half a day on mods for this, because even after installing a mod for ARROW KEYS, the keyboard conflicts with some other action that is not in the keybinding option anyway. 
Fix your rebinding options and I will buy again.

Soul crushing.  I can NOT believe in 2026 that developers have locked hard binds to WASD or... anything!  There HAS to be a way to tell these guys that people need bindable controls EVEN IF it's not for Accessibility purposes.  I am in complete disbelief that an $80 game that HAS a hidden keybind screen in the options, but blocked or locked basic movement keys.
It's so disappointing when studios are so lazy that won't let you rebind movement keys

The directional keys and some others are hardlocked. I'm not bothering to get third party systems to play a game I have nothing invested in. Full remappable keybinds should be basic practice by now. Even indie developers usually have them. Didn't even get to play the game because it's not accessible without custom keybinds. Definitely a "me" problem, but one I think major developers should have the forsight to plan for. So, can't recommend something that blocks me from playing from the jump.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the controls feel clunky, awkward, or unintuitive, with poorly mapped default button layouts.

citations.review_text: I have never regretted buying a game more than this one.  The controls are wonky to the point of frustration and the first boss in the quarry was completely unkillable even on the easy setting.  I gave up fighting him after like the 20th reset.  I'm not a god gamer.  I'm old and just want to enjoy the game casually and that is what easy was listed as but holy crap it was a lie.  I have completely lost interest in playing anymore.  If i could refund I would.

11/10. Just a really great game all around—the world looks amazing and the whole thing just feels really well made. My only real struggle so far is the controls, they're definitely pretty hard to get the hang of at first. Works flawlessly on Bazzite Linux too, which is awesome. Only at 10.7 hours right now, so check back after some months when I'm sitting at 2,000h+.

It has soooo much promise, but the controls are _so_ bad that I just can't enjoy the game at all. In combat I'm fighting the controls more than the enemies. And out of combat it feels like it always tries to do the wrong thing with the button that I'm pressing, since the targetting changes so wildly.

Like running and starting talking are the same button, so when I run by the barber, I always start a conversation with them.
When trying to read a poster, I keep turning the lantern next to it on/off, because it's the same button.

I just can't.

Its a shame but the controls on keyboard are bad. They added some options to tweak it to be ok but not enough. In combat its a bit clunky but not bad and you can get used to it, but just walking around the world feels bad. They don't even give an option to use hold to run, you can't remap wasd movement, you have way too much forward momentum, even jumping is so clunky you have to use a special aim to actually be able to jump accurately and countless tiny little things that add up and you need to push through. You can eventually get used to it but you have to unlearn like basically every other game and even then movement is just slightly inferior to like all other games. Its a constant nagging irritation you need to live with. 

I had heard about the controls but I thought it was more that you needed to learn some advanced moves which I've done with other games and was prepared for, but its not the complex moves that are too hard its just that the very basic fundamentals just don't feel quite right. Its like if the sound design had just a very faint beeping noise in the background, not a dealbreaker but a small constant annoyance. The devs are certainly very active in tweaks though so maybe one day they will get around to this, but my fear is that because they already tweaked the movement some they think its good enough. Its probably a bit better on controller but this is a heads-up for people on keyboard and mouse.

Who the hell thought those controls were a good idea. They aren't even consistent across input devices. 

An example: Shooting your bow. With MKB you hold Q (Q??? Wat?) to draw your bow, and click to shoot. So far, only a bit weird. On controller you'd think it would be similar. Left trigger to draw the bow, right trigger or RB to shoot. Right? RIGHT? No, you release the left trigger and it shoots. 

What the actual hell...

And don't get me started on the Weapon-Wheel. F2 on PC? Are you serious? F2? Why not Tab like every other game in existence? 

There are plenty more examples, but these should give you a good glimpse into the madness.


I'm sorry, but whoever designed those controls, you seriously need to play a few more games before you ever work on one again. 

You made a square wheel, and by god am I mad that I broke the 2 hour limit by trying to understand those shitty controls.

The apologists that defend the controls with "you have to learn them", Wheels are round for a reason. No amount of learning will ever make square wheels okay.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the game requires players to sit through long, forced introductory missions and exposition before reaching the open world.

citations.review_text:
I put off buying this for ages and finally bought it.

The forced intro missions are excruciating. I'm four hours in and still following them. I can't express how little I care about the story at this point. They've introduced a dozen character, multiple plot threads, and the forced following for nonskippable exposition takes ages.

I've heard too many good things about the game to not keep trying, but it's going to take me a good week of playing an hour or two at a time to get through the introduction. And they keep introducing mechanics that are then not used. Every mechanic has its own keyboard combination you have to memorize, and when they don't use a mechanic consistently I forget them and have to look them up again. I spent twenty minutes trying to remember how to raise my lantern to catch a memory fragment or whatever it is.

Maybe I'm not the core demographic. ADHD makes it difficult for me to deal with things like this. Or maybe I'm just spoiled by games like Dragonwilds and Enshrouded where you just jump directly into things without forced exposition.

I wish there were a 'meh' recommendation. I can see why people like it, but until I get past the intro and experience the proper game I can't recommend it. Maybe I'll just download a save game from somewhere.

I've never played such a wierd mess of a game - at least in starfield i could find SOME fun ... this is just unimmersive and meaningless nonsense strung together, every game ever successful was just copied and often badly, the protagonist is preset in every concieveable way, and a paragon of virtue and goodness, and yet there is massive amounts of mechanics to be a bad person.. what for? 

Can't even refund this mess because if you're nice to the game and keep giving it a chance to proof to you that its worthwhile to continue you spend so much time walking around doing nonsense and looking at slow cutscenes or other barriers youre way beyond 2 hours

Its honestly baffling to me how developers can craft such a wonderful looking world make it seem interesting fill it with lore and then ruin it by locking you out of the openworld, out of roleplay, out of freedom.
There is no reason to engage with most of the game if you take Kliff serious as a character, you can't make your own character you can't play the other 2 until youve spend over 20 hours aparantly... what in the world is this game meant to be?

claims.claim: Reviewers note that visual settings and lighting cause issues such as excessive contrast, heavy blurriness requiring upscaling or ray reconstruction, and poor visibility during nighttime or in dark areas.

citations.review_text:
You need at least an RTX 5070 to have a decent experience. I would personally recommend an RTX 5080.

The game looks extremely blurry, even at 4K with DLSS. The only solution I found was enabling Ray Reconstruction, but it comes at a massive cost: around 50% performance loss. It significantly reduces the blurriness and improves lighting in outdoor areas. However, indoor environments become a mess, with houses looking like they're made of metal, covered in a flat, gray appearance.

Pop-in is also present, but honestly, it was one of the least concerning issues for me.

On the CPU side, I would recommend at least a Ryzen 7 5700X3D if you want a consistent 60 FPS, especially during large-scale battles where the game has to handle a massive number of NPCs.

My recommendation: Only consider buying this game if you have a genuinely powerful PC. Otherwise, you're likely to end up playing one of the blurriest games ever made.

Games that rely too heavily on TAA and upscaling techniques tend to suffer from this problem. Unfortunately, this has become a recurring issue with modern games, particularly those built on Unreal Engine 5.
Fun game in many ways - in daytime environments. Once it gets dark anywhere the lighting is so bad it can be unplayable in some places. Stopped playing because of it - please Pearl Abyss, fix this.

Since its release, Crimson Desert has been getting praised left and right, and maybe I'm in the minority here, but I find the game's lighting to be a seriously frustrating flaw.

The excessive contrast makes the game look downright ugly at times, to the point where my eyes start hurting after just half an hour. Shadows under open-sided tents are so dark that NPCs look like pitch-black silhouettes, while direct sunlight can be so intense that you can barely make out their faces. The grass is another issue, often looking almost neon green and completely oversaturated.

And it's not like these problems are hard to spot. That ridiculously green grass is right there in the official trailers and screenshots, even on Steam.  Honestly, I'm practically praying for foggy weather sometimes, because that's probably when Crimson Desert looks its best.

I've seen plenty of people suggesting that players adjust the brightness and contrast, but none of those tweaks seem to fix the problem. Instead, we're left relying on modders to address these issues, and with patches coming out so frequently, keeping those mods working is a hassle in itself.

It's frustrating to see the developers continue to pump out content instead of properly polishing the experience. At this rate, you'll be able to start a family and spend your entire life in the game before they get around to fixing the basics. No matter how many patches, content updates, or expansions they release, none of that matters much if the game itself is still so unpleasant to look at.

That said, I completely understand why people enjoy it. If the lighting didn't bother me so much, I could easily see myself getting sucked into the game too. But in its current state, I simply can't recommend it to anyone. Crimson Desert has plenty of potential, but for me, the visuals are a dealbreaker.

I will start by saying that I do not like Pearl Abyss.
As a result, I was opposed to this game from the start.
I didn't know much about it, but it looked like a slop, mashup, cash-grab that I was sure would be riddled with microtransactions.

I had the chance to try the game for free and I figured "why not?".
After a little while, I reached the start of the open world and some of the intro/tutorial quests and started to see the systems in place. I was blown away. I ended up buying it myself.

There does not seem to be a way to skip most dialog, instead you can hold a button to fast forward through it.
I ended up liking this more than I thought I would. I typically skip cuscenes and dialog because they take too long. I liked that I could get all of the info and story, but without having to wade through hours of people talking at each other.

The story and characters are OK. Not great, just OK.
The boss fights are pretty cool. Not on the difficulty of dark souls, but still quite a challenge.
There is a camp you an upgrade and stock, and companion dispatch missions you can do to influence the world.
There are so many puzzles. Some can be quite archaic, but not too bad at all. just look one up if you don't want to do it, it's not that deep.

The controls are kinda bad. 
They are usable, but there are lots of functions bound to the same buttons, or button combos that are hard to remember in the heat of the moment when you need them.  You get used to them, but I wouldn't say any of them are really intuitive.

There are no microtransactions. 
The only additional money you can give is for deluxe edition which includes some cosmetics, or a "DLC/Expansion" releasing later this month, which looks to be a sizable content addition. This is in stark contrast to what I expected knowing Pearl Abyss.

They released an "enhanced edition" only a few months after launch which feels odd, but its basically just an upgrade patch to the base game. No additional charge or anything. They add…

I played Crimson Desert when it first launched in March, and I was absolutely blown away. The graphics, the world, the atmosphere — everything looked incredible.

How is it even possible for a game to look worse after several updates? What happened?

citations.review_text:
My favorite open world game ever as someone who generally doesn't like them, a personal 9/10. However, this game will not appeal to most modern videogame players. The characters and story are awful and you need to be comfortable with undirected gameplay where the carrot on a stick is the gameplay itself, not some reward at the end of doing something you otherwise wouldn't want to do. (Although there are indeed plenty of rewards to chase.) The world being very beautiful and detailed with little things to collect from mundane to exotic helps encourage exploration a ton.

The DLC added more of the same. The world feels more alive than it did before now that there's ships and PoIs on the horizon. (I thought it was already great when the game released and it's even better now.) If you liked the base game, you'll like the DLC, but it won't change your opinion of the game from what it already was.

[b]Crimson Desert[/b] - a very engaging and enjoyable sandbox adventure that doesn't tell you how to have fun. It gives you an enormous open world filled with mysteries, secrets, and an incredible variety of gameplay mechanics. There's always something to discover or something new to try, and it's surprisingly easy to get distracted for hours while simply exploring the world.
[h3]What’s Good:[/h3]
[list]
[*]An incredible amount of different mechanics and activities. Fishing, hunting, farming, cooking, trading, running businesses, building, gambling, and much more. There's almost always something to do, even when you're not following the main quests.
[*]Almost complete freedom of action. The game doesn't hold your hand or constantly tell you what to do. You're free to explore, experiment, and spend your time however you want.
[*]Beautiful graphics. The game looks absolutely gorgeous, with detailed environments, impressive landscapes, and plenty of beautiful visual effects.
[*]Pleasant soundtrack and sound effects. Plenty of enjoyable musical compositions that complement the visuals, while environmental sounds and interaction effects help bring the world to life.
[*]Beautiful and diverse visual design. From character appearances and armor sets to weapons, architecture, settlements, and landscapes, there's a lot of visual variety. Different regions and equipment have their own distinctive styles, making the world enjoyable to explore and simply look at.
[*]An enormous open world. The world is genuinely huge, and exploring it can easily take hundreds of hours. You can set out to complete a quest and end up spending several hours exploring a cave, discovering a hidden chest, solving a puzzle, or getting distracted by an entire chain of side quests, eventually forgetting where you were originally heading.
[*]A huge number of secrets. Hidden passages, treasure chests, puzzles, unusual locations, and other discoveries with rewards provide plenty of reasons to explore every …

The game certainly had a rough launch, but Pearl Abyss absolutely delivered. All the updates and free content added in such a short amount of time is an anomaly in this video game era. This game's world is amazing and feels alive. 

The Charting the Unknown DLC added a ton more content that is a blend of Subnautica, Windrose/Assassin's Creed Black Flag, The Sims, and Civilization. The seafaring gameplay rivals Windrose and Assassin's Creed Black Flag despite this game not solely focused on sailing and pirate or naval lifestyle. The home and base mechanics added with this DLC also can compete with The Sims. I found the underwater exploration quite exciting. This is my game of the year.

It's okay for a sandbox game, the graphics and engine make the environment really pretty to look at. 

The controls are some of the loosest I've played in a game made in the last decade or two, combat is either 1 vs 100 Dynasty Warriors stuff where you're mowing down endless waves of hapless idiots, or boss fights that range from almost fun to frustrating in the worst types of ways. It's pretty half baked either way, which is what most of this game ultimately feels like. Cool concepts, with the follow through being not that polished. 6/10 if I'm being generous on that front. 

Exploration, it looks pretty. Flying around the map is pretty fun, riding around in horses and wagons and the like was janky enough on top of the fact that I could just fly to my destination that I never interacted with that sort of mechanic unless it was absolutely forced on me. You get a dragon on the tail end of the main story and that was neat I guess. Thing is, as neat as riding a dragon is, the missions involving you flying it around to take out the bosses involved were just more of the game showing it's ass to me in terms of how tedious, unintuitive, and annoying it could be. There's a lot of cool stuff and loot hidden out in the open world to make it worth your time somewhat to just go and fuck around in the sandbox aspect. Honestly where this game shines the most because the story is dull and tacked on as an afterthought, so don't expect much there. 7/10 

Story 0/10 I started playing with something to keep me awake on my second monitor after getting through the opening hours because this shit is dry. Good guy random chosen one archetype mysteriously chosen by mentor archetypes who live in the sky to stop generic evil people who want to take over the world. This stuff was written as an afterthought so it really doesn't bear mentioning too much on the game overall except that it asserts itself too much into the experience. 

This probably just isn't a game for me. Fans of this …

This is the best open world sandbox game in a long time, the progression feels pretty good. The update in 2.0 solved a lot of the story issues, which whilst still the weakest part, the rest of the game makes up for it.

I struggle reviewing this game. In terms of graphics, worldbuilding, features, and combat schematics, it's magnificent. There's a decent sense of progression and the exploration opportunities are near-endless. 

The game's replayability, however, suffers from stale writing and narrative cohesion. Quests--and the abundance of quests available--can appear inconsequential to the greater world within the game, reducing immersion over time. The characters are cliched (not necessarily an issue, given the genre), the dialogue is repetitive, and the game's pacing feels both too fast and too slow.

Nonetheless, I recommend this game if you can buy it on sale. The fun wears off; however, the game's gorgeous and massive.

Crimson Desert – My Game of the Year 2026, Flaws and All

Crimson Desert is one of the most ambitious open-world games I've ever played, and easily my Game of the Year 2026. It's also an occasionally overwhelming, frustrating, and somewhat messy experience. But despite its shortcomings, what Pearl Abyss has achieved here is nothing short of remarkable.

First of all, the sheer scale of the game is staggering. Pywel is an absolutely gigantic world, packed with potentially hundreds of hours of content. The environments are incredibly diverse, ranging from lush forests and towering mountains to vast deserts, bustling cities, and now even the depths of the ocean. The world is visually stunning, and there's a genuine sense of adventure around almost every corner.

Exploration is particularly rewarding. Unlike many open-world games where discovering a hidden location often leads to some generic crafting materials, Crimson Desert regularly rewards curiosity with meaningful loot: unique weapons, armor pieces, accessories, Abyss Gear, and countless other discoveries. There's always something worth investigating, and the game rarely makes you feel like you've wasted your time wandering off the beaten path.

However, that ambition comes at a cost.

Crimson Desert features an almost absurd number of gameplay systems and mechanics. Combat, crafting, exploration, environmental puzzles, camp management, and countless other activities are all crammed into the same game. It's an impressive achievement, but also something of a patchwork that can be intimidating and difficult to fully grasp.

Some abilities and mechanics are introduced only to remain unused for hours, sometimes even longer. By the time you encounter a puzzle requiring a specific interaction, there's a good chance you've completely forgotten that you could perform that action in the first place. The game occasionally seems to expect players to remember everything they've learned, regardless of how rarely th…

★★★★★ Crimson Desert is a masterpiece, and I can’t stop thinking about it

I loved every minute of Crimson Desert. It’s one of the best open-world action-adventure games I’ve ever played, and it’s easily one of the standouts of this generation.

The combat is incredible. It’s fast, physical and brutal. Every hit has weight, and there’s real freedom in how you fight. Progression gives you new attacks and abilities instead of dull stat bumps, so you’re always learning something new. Bosses feel like events, and mastering the combat is deeply rewarding.

Pywel is a jaw-dropping world. The visuals are spectacular. The landscapes, weather and lighting make the screenshots look like concept art. The world is huge and packed with things to do, and I kept getting sidetracked by something I spotted on the horizon. Exploration here is pure joy.

It respects your freedom. This game gives you a sandbox and trusts you to enjoy it. There’s a lot of variety in the activities, systems and surprises. It feels like a world made by people who love open-world games.

The verdict: Crimson Desert is ambitious, beautiful and endlessly fun. It’s a game I’d happily sink hundreds more hours into. If you love open worlds and great combat, play it.

10/10. Absolutely phenomenal.

This game is the elder scrolls we have been waiting for. Literally something for everyone. Enormous open world with so many bugs, animals creatures, and pets. Literally so many pets. Combat is amazing. Story is amazing. A BILLION side quests! So many different mechanics and things to do in the game

claims.claim: Reviewers report that puzzles and progression can be obscure or frustrating, frequently requiring external guides or walkthroughs.

citations.review_text: The game is complex, frequently requiring YouTube  or other sources for hints, but it is a massive, beautiful open world story with a great deal of depth and texture, and amazingly smooth loading as you move across terrain There are all kinds of story lines to follow, and plenty of opportunities for mad fights.

a map packed full of things to discover, hunt and collect. enemy encounters are fun and bosses can be a challenge. the puzzles are great but some can be a bit confusing on how they're meant to be solved. The grind for resources is fun and there are many other mechanics to discover that can make some things easier to do. its just a blast.

This game started off strong, and somehow managed to get even better as I progressed. Unfortunately, what began as an enjoyable experience eventually turned into an absolute slog. 6/10. And honestly, the biggest culprit was the goddamn puzzles.

I'm not exaggerating when I say that roughly 70% of these puzzles had me opening YouTube just to figure out what the hell I was supposed to do. There's a difference between challenging players and making them feel like they need a PhD to progress. A puzzle should reward your ability to think, not force you to abandon the game and consult a walkthrough every five minutes. At some point, the frustration completely outweighs the satisfaction.

And then Chapter 11 happened. Whatever goodwill the game had built up started evaporating as I found myself fighting endless waves of robotic enemies. The experience became repetitive, tedious, and downright boring. It was as if the game had run out of interesting ideas and decided that throwing more enemies at me was an acceptable substitute for engaging gameplay.

But the final mission in the Abyss? That was the final nail in the coffin.

I had to solve yet another goddamn puzzle just to reach Caliburn, the final boss. And how long did I spend on that one puzzle? AN ENTIRE HOUR!. By the time I finally made it to the boss, whatever excitement I might have felt had completely disappeared. I didn't care about the spectacle. I didn't care about the confrontation. I didn't even care about enjoying the final fight.

I just wanted to kill the Final boss, finish the game, and get the hell out.

Think about that for a second: the game had worn me down so badly that reaching the final boss felt less like a reward and more like being released from captivity. I wasn't playing because I was having fun anymore; I was playing because I'd already invested so much time that I might as well see it through to the end.

And that's what makes this so disappointing. The game had a strong start, built genuine…

Game is fine. Problem is the ui and controls are made by aliens that barely understand how humans play video games. At least this is the only sane reason i can manage with to understand how ideas like stupid helmets for everything,  obscure puzzles   without explanation which mechanic to use, menus and ui can be made that weird. It's not even bad - it's alien to human way of comprehending things.

So, i wish the team will find a human consultant who will help them to understand human logic and how games are actually made to be played comfortably.

citations.review_text:
I just read one of the top negative reviews that in summary said something like CD (Crimson Desert) is a decent MMO packaged as a singleplayer game that doesn't deliver any one thing very well and it's not something resembling the Witcher or an Elder Scrolls game, etc,- I mostly agreed with the essence of what the reviewer had to say. That being said, I also feel so strongly in the positive direction about some of these same things and the game more broadly, and after playing for over 100 hours, reading that negative review urged me to write this positive one explaining the difference in my mind.

As most negative and positive reviews alike aptly state, the controls suck. It's really remarkable sometimes, actually, just how much they suck when the rest of the game doesn't suck. I'm also leading with it because of just how bad the controls suck. This has to be understood before trying to take this game on. I look around in this game at the BEAUTIFUL landscape and trees and grass and rocks and mountains and distant forts and castles and spires etc etc etc just non stop amazing scenes in the most vivid color driven by the most rich lighting system I've ever seen anywhere, and it's truly amazing, and the quests I can choose between sound really fun and I'm looking forward to really sweet boss fights with rad new weapons and armor that I can admire and maybe upgrade and spec with really sweet abilities that are usually actually strong and impactful while maintaining identity between the different ones without getting trivial or redundant, and the boss fights themselves is fun, even if the occasional boss design isn't the most original thing ever thought up (it isn't a crime to make a big strong warrior human with big sword as a boss), and the variety in combat options is great BUT, after all this awesome stuff, we got to the problem. We encountered gameplay, and it's immediately hindered by the controls being so so bad. I have to go to the boss by moving, with the contro…

It's okay for a sandbox game, the graphics and engine make the environment really pretty to look at. 

The controls are some of the loosest I've played in a game made in the last decade or two, combat is either 1 vs 100 Dynasty Warriors stuff where you're mowing down endless waves of hapless idiots, or boss fights that range from almost fun to frustrating in the worst types of ways. It's pretty half baked either way, which is what most of this game ultimately feels like. Cool concepts, with the follow through being not that polished. 6/10 if I'm being generous on that front. 

Exploration, it looks pretty. Flying around the map is pretty fun, riding around in horses and wagons and the like was janky enough on top of the fact that I could just fly to my destination that I never interacted with that sort of mechanic unless it was absolutely forced on me. You get a dragon on the tail end of the main story and that was neat I guess. Thing is, as neat as riding a dragon is, the missions involving you flying it around to take out the bosses involved were just more of the game showing it's ass to me in terms of how tedious, unintuitive, and annoying it could be. There's a lot of cool stuff and loot hidden out in the open world to make it worth your time somewhat to just go and fuck around in the sandbox aspect. Honestly where this game shines the most because the story is dull and tacked on as an afterthought, so don't expect much there. 7/10 

Story 0/10 I started playing with something to keep me awake on my second monitor after getting through the opening hours because this shit is dry. Good guy random chosen one archetype mysteriously chosen by mentor archetypes who live in the sky to stop generic evil people who want to take over the world. This stuff was written as an afterthought so it really doesn't bear mentioning too much on the game overall except that it asserts itself too much into the experience. 

This probably just isn't a game for me. Fans of this …

Absolutely one of my favorite games of all time. The closest game I can compare it to is Breath of the wild, but for adults. This game doesn't hold your hand and makes you find it/ figure it out yourself. The exploration and views are best in the business. Combat is good but don't expect Dark Souls. The only complaints I have is the controls are a bit jank and you need to take your time using them. THERE IS NOT ENOUGH STORAGE!!!! I like to collect and hoard, I wish there were more storage options. At least for collecting gear. Over all best game and will be a long time before someone else comes close to how bad a** this game is. If you like Zelda BOTW, Skyrim or Witcher 3, Open world exploration, fun puzzles/games, or beautiful views then this game is for you. Get it!

Rated for its big sandbox open-world, this game is an easy YES. It is incredibly impressive how much attention to detail and passion has gone into creating the world of Crimson Desert! But gameplay-wise, and as a "roundup deliberate experience", its sadly a NO.

A seamless open world with no boundaries is awesome. But when this approach starts breaking its own quest system and game mechanics, it becomes a problem. Exploring, wandering around, and just minding your own business in Crimson Desert is incredible. Playing through the main story and questing in general, however, fucking sucks. You get stuck regularly during progression and sometimes have to reload an older save because the heavily scripted quest system keeps tripping over its own feet and cant comprehend all the different ways you could tackle a very vague mission-objective! 
Its incredibly frustrating when youre running around a quest area, trying to figure out what youre supposed to do, only to discover that youve missed some obscure world trigger or failed to complete certain actions in a specific order (without the game ever telling you that, btw)! Thank you youtube!

The 2nd part of the problem is the controls, and I dont think they are fixable in any way! Youre one step away from playing "Manual Samuel". Movement/combat/world interaction feels like youre in an F1 car simulation while the game world is playing Mario Kart + throwing bananas at you. Normally, I play these kinds of games with a controller, but the button layout (double and triple button assignments + hold-press inputs) was so bad that I switched to mouse + keyboard – and even that sucked to play with. For example, you have to input a sequence of 5 different buttons + double and long presses, just to move around in the world... Let that sink in.

And then there are Quite a bit puzzles in this game, where all weak points of Crimson Desert come together. Now you have to not only figure out what to do, but how to interact with it.  Rotating…
